en: Preface to the *Jingtu yi jue* (Decisions on the Pure Land):
The moon appears in a thousand rivers when the water is still and clear; the wind arises over the four seas, stirring the waves into turbidity.

It is because the waves move that the wind is perceived, and because the water is still that the moon is revealed. How could it be that the ocean is turbid when the waves are still, while the river is clear when the water moves? Such is the nature of the land.

The distinction between purity and defilement is likewise so: when one awakens to the Buddha-way, the land is adorned as a Pure Land; when the ordinary mind is deluded, it is a defective land of defilement.

It is clear that it is not the case that the land is pure while the mind is deluded or the land is defiled while the mind is awakened. If one wishes to be born in the Pure Land, one must first seek awakening.
For awakening can be accommodated even within the defilement of birth and death; thus, Amitābha is translated as "Immeasurable Life."

The measure of immeasurable light takes "reception" as its meaning. When mindfulness of the Buddha reaches the mind such that it is no longer distracted, both the perceptions of the holy and the common are no longer received;

one directly attains the state where even the jeweled trees and net-like canopies are nothing other than the recitation of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—this is precisely what is called the inconceivable "insentient beings preaching the Dharma. Realizing this non-reception through correspondence is termed the "function of longevity."

This cannot be accommodated [by mere conceptualization]; it is transformed and termed "light" (*ābhāsa*), which carries two meanings. Thus, its Sanskrit original has been retained for the sake of circulation.

Is the Pure Land and Amitābha not simply the fundamental nature of the mind? The venerable elder master Beichan and our former teacher, Xianshi of Sanfeng, were most harmonious in their spiritual resonance.
Having exhausted the inner sanctum [of the teachings] through years of diligent study, our former teacher passed away.
Later, those who responded to his teachings became rare; he nurtured the Way, rested his mind, and settled his body within Amitābha’s Pure Land, like a dragon in hiding that "does not act.
Yet, how could it be otherwise? When the spring thunder stirs in due season, one cannot avoid emerging to raise the clouds.

Thus, he unleashed the celestial rain of his own nature upon the Pure Land, and having already composed a single volume on the essence of the Lotus School, he struck out its core until it was exhausted, from ancient times down to the present.
Among the commentaries and sub-commentaries, numbering no fewer than several dozen, none can surpass this work in essentiality or difficulty;
it is not only that it shares the same track with the teachings of Jetavana, but even the single-lineage transmission of Shaolin follows its same wind without deviation.
As Yongming said, "To possess both Chan and Pure Land is like a horned tiger"—is this not what he meant? Since this is now the final parting word, I intend to elaborate upon it.
I have already parted with this teaching from others and intend to entrust it to the carvers to ensure its wide circulation and preservation;

I thus preface it with these few words as an introduction. I am ashamed that I lack the literary skill to praise it, yet within the aspiration to assist in the transformation of beings, I could not refuse.
Therefore, turning toward another peak, I shall directly address it: if one says there is no "parting instruction" (訣) to be obtained, this is itself called "obtaining."
The Parting Instruction: Shall we say it is already a parting, or is it not yet a parting? I am unable to add further description to this.

On the day before the final day of the eleventh month in the Renwu year of the Chongzhen era, Sanfeng Hongzheng held a colloquial discussion on the Pure Land and inscribed this as "The Parting Instruction."
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty;
explained by the Śramaṇa Dahui of Beichansi Temple in Wumen, Ming Dynasty.
*The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha*.
In the Sanskrit language, Amitābha is translated here as "Immeasurable Life" (Wuliangshou) and also as "Immeasurable Light" (Wuliangguang).

When the Buddha speaks of him, it is our World-Honored One of this land praising that Buddha’s name and the excellence of his original vows, employing various skillful means to guide and lead all sentient beings.
Thus, "immeasurable" refers to number when speaking of his life-span being immeasurable, and refers to principle when speaking of his light.
This is because the mind is immeasurable. Why? Because all sentient beings abide within the essence of the immeasurable;
as soon as a single thought arises, within that single thought, birth, abiding, change, and cessation are fully present, forming the four applications of mindfulness.
These thoughts proliferate successively into the immeasurable, yet they revolve within a single thought. Thus, a single thought is complete with the inconceivable and the unutterable.
It is said that the Spirit uses radiance to illumine the lands of the ten directions; this is called Immeasurable Light.

If sentient beings, relying upon the essence of the immeasurable, give rise to even a single thought, within this single thought, pervasive conceptualization immediately becomes manifold thoughts, and thereupon immeasurable births and deaths arise.
This is the gate of transmigration (*pravṛtti*). If, however, one is within the gate of cessation and return (*nivṛtti*), as for the mind and consciousness—
Because consciousness cannot reach it, it is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*); it is also the ultimate limit of calculation. Thus, immeasurable numbers regress:

ten thousand return to ten thousand, ten thousand return to one thousand, one thousand return to one hundred, one hundred return to ten, and ten return to one. One does not know where that one returns; therefore, it is termed "immeasurable.
Only when the minds of both the holy and the ordinary are thus exhausted does the entirety of the ten directions become the Pure Land—this is what is meant by "immeasurable."

Life is the essence; immeasurable light is its function. This single phrase, "Immeasurable Light," encompasses both the eastern and western lands throughout the entirety of the empty dharma-realm as one single sentence. In Amitābha Buddha, there is no further dharma remaining. Why is this?
Because the mind is immeasurable, the world is also immeasurable—this is what is called the Dharma-realm Treasury Body of Amitābha.

"Buddha-Buddha" is translated as "Awakened. It is that both the ignorant and the wise possess it; yet, alas, because the sentiments of ordinary beings and sages are separated, they are unable to enter into pure awakening.
If both the sage and the ordinary being were to be obliterated, it would constitute nihilism; if they were mixed together without distinction, it would also be called confusion.
Only when one is free from these manifold words and all ten realms of existence are realized as the perfect nature of awakening is it truly so.
The teaching that can be said to correspond to all capacities may also be called the *Sarvākārajñatā-sūtra*.

Just as water moistening the great earth has not lost its original source but continues to flow, so too the teachings of the Buddhas from beginning to end employ the source of a single sūtra to penetrate the vital circulation.
Those Buddha-sūtras, throughout immeasurable kalpas, speak solely of this one [truth].
Does this single character of the sutra encompass all phenomena, or does it not? It is said that the ten thousand myriad *koṭis* of *yojanas* are traversed even during the time of eating.
If one contemplates the actual reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the causes and conditions of the Pure Land with true insight, how could these be expressed by words?
Yet, apart from words, how could such a thing exist? Although wisdom transcends old expressions, the new ones are likewise [transcended].
The remaining names and characteristics beyond these central phrases have already been explained in detail by previous commentators; therefore, I shall set them aside and not describe them here.

Having now resolved this, I will explain only a single phrase: according to the precedent of the ancient *Amitābha-sūtra*, both the sentient and the insentient are equally complete and lacking nothing.
The six characters of this sutra’s title, as well as phrases such as "Thus have I heard," are merely the compiler’s way of connecting the flow of the text.
Thus have I heard... (up to) together with an immeasurable assembly of devas.
Regarding "Thus have I heard": Ānanda personally heard it so as to sever doubt and give rise to faith. Regarding "at one time":
when the World-Honored One spoke this sutra, three times constitute one time; this may serve as the essential for preaching the Dharma, awakening the three minds.
Mie said: "The 'Buddha' and the 'Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika Park' are the locations where the Dharma is preached;
they are not talk about emptiness or formlessness. Within the realm of phenomenal appearances (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), there are indeed substantial dharmas. This is to manifest that there is no falsehood.
Because the human mind flows and pours forth, it must abide within a single atom; only when the minds of both sages and ordinary beings are exhausted can one attain Suchness."
At one time, there was a great manifestation. The assembly of bhikṣus and great bodhisattvas were those who had formerly followed the multitude.

This demonstrates the principle of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*): the Dharma that is preached does not arise from the Buddha, nor does it arise from the bhikṣus, nor does it arise from the Buddha, the bhikṣus, the bodhisattvas, and the devas acting together; rather, it arises because of the deluded sentient beings of this land. Therefore...

It is not that all sentient beings arise without cause; rather, with ignorance as a condition there are volitional formations, and so on, up to birth as a condition for old age and death—all these arise from conditions and, because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are said to be unarisen.

The physical, verbal, and mental karma of all noble ones and ordinary beings, as well as the dharma-realm, arise from earth, water, fire, wind, and space. Thus, each of these five great elements arises [from its own causes].
Because that which arises through conditions lacks intrinsic nature, it is therefore said to be unarisen. All sentient beings and insentient things dwell together in the primordial limit;
the three periods of time are fundamentally illusory and lack intrinsic nature, and thus are called "unborn. This is the essential meaning of the Unborn Pure Land:
while the ignorant are hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds away, the wise have it before their eyes. Although the Buddha points toward the West, it is like using an elephant as a metaphor.

Why is it that all things and phenomena in this land are fully encompassed? Because every single thing and every single phenomenon in this land possesses the entirety of the Great Dharma Treasury from beginning to end; for every dharma is produced through causes and conditions.

If one analyzes even a mere inch of earth until birth is seen as empty and turns within that emptiness, and further reaches the state where both illumination and cessation are simultaneous—this perfect clarity is the entry into non-arising.
Furthermore, there is another kind of sentient being who, amidst even a single inch of soil, does not require the gradual progression of practice;
through the secret contemplation of non-arising, non-ceasing, no coming, and no going, they suddenly enter the wondrous purport of the Perfect Sound in a single kṣaṇa.
This is what is meant by saying that the World-Honored One’s forty-nine years of Dharma were all expounded at once. It can be seen that such people exist.
Every person is Amitāyus; every object is Amitābha’s light; every word is a lotus flower; every step is a realm of golden light.
The four sufferings are all *Sukhāvatī*; the eight difficulties are all the Pure Land. In the basin of the pure hands lies the water of eight virtues;
as birds sing and the wind blows through the trees, they expound the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*). For those who have not yet attained this, employ a single phrase of Amitābha.

The Buddha cuts off the myriad streams moment by moment; eventually, there comes a time when he reaches the point of cessation. Why does this sutra contain passages spoken ex cathedra without being requested?
First, because the disciples here lack the karmic conditions for it, [the Buddha] points directly to the bliss of the Western Land to inspire their aspiration.
Second, because there was no one present who was a suitable vessel, he therefore addressed Śāriputra with these instructions.
For this reason, he wishes to cause the great assembly present here to suddenly realize the phrase "Immeasurable Light.
To speak in this manner is a swift means for sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age to transcend birth and death; otherwise, it would merely be a matter of expedient teachings remaining as mere earth.
The section on the introductory narrative (序分, xùfēn) is now concluded; what follows is called the section on the main teaching (正宗分, zhèngzōngfēn).
At that time, the Buddha spoke [up to] "preaching the Dharma even now.

There is a world named Sukhāvatī; in that land, the secondary retribution (the environment) is adorned, and Amitābha currently preaches the Dharma there, adorned with the primary retribution (the physical marks and signs).
"Sukhāvatī" is the designation for the complete perfection of both the primary and secondary retributions.
This is the great meaning of the entire sutra: that from this land to that land, across hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds, one ascends to that country in less than a moment.

This is the principle within the Buddha-land; such is the Buddha-land. When practice and manifestation are both pervasive and interfused, it is the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle, and the non-obstruction between all phenomena. If one examines this in detail, it clarifies a single "A" [the letter A].

The seed-syllables can only emerge when the mind is free from delusion; thus, there is no falsehood. As for Amitābha preaching the Dharma in the present, it has been ten kalpas since that Buddha attained enlightenment.
Not only ten kalpas, but since beginningless time, throughout the entirety of that Buddha’s lifespan, he may also be considered as being in the "present" at this very moment.
What is the meaning of this? It is because the ultimate limit (the *koṭi*) has no prior point.
Because of the future limit, there is only the single moment of the present. If it were not so, then even from one day up to seven days would merely be a provisional means;

only upon being born in that land does one first realize that Amitābha Buddha and I are born together, and even that all Buddhas of the past, future, and present are likewise born with me and preach the Dharma together.
Because they do not depart from the dharma of abiding as it originally was, it is said that they preach the Dharma simultaneously.
Śāriputra... [up to] ...therefore it is named "Ultimate Bliss.
That land is called "Ultimate Bliss" in contrast to the extreme suffering of this land; although the sentient beings of this land suffer, [the former is blissful].

Because they do not yet resolve their minds [for enlightenment], he points toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss to cause people to delight in and aspire to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, taking "single-mindedness without confusion" as the cause and the realization of the inconceivable body as the fruit.

As for "Ultimate Bliss," it is free from the suffering of this land; bliss is merely a provisional name, yet it is called true bliss. The following text clarifies its immeasurable and ultimate nature.

It is the essence of bliss. Furthermore, Śāriputra... [omitted] ...for this reason it is called "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*). (The adornments of that land originally have nothing to indicate them; whether foolish or wise, they appear as pure or defiled according to their karma.
Things are not indicated by the mind, nor are they the mind itself. Since both mind and things are non-existent, only the mind can manifest them.)
Regarding the "sevenfold railings" and so forth, there is a difficult question: Do these sevenfold [railings] belong to a single person, or to a single world-system?
Are they possessed by the Buddha alone? If they belong to a single person, it cannot be established [as a universal feature].

If they belong to the Buddha alone, what concern does this have with the people of that land? This applies equally to the "four treasures surrounding [the land]" and so on. The answer is: It is not so.
Furthermore, because the seven consciousnesses shared by Buddhas and sentient beings are identical in purity with the *tathāgatagarbha*,
and because the eight consciousnesses of sentient beings are all subsumed within a single moment of the wondrous functioning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
it is solely due to the fact that the preceding seven consciousnesses give rise to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing in succession that they are not pure.

However, when the seven and eight [consciousnesses] merge into a single essence, free from the prior and subsequent attachments of parikalpita (imagined nature), this is precisely the ever-quiescent *dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm).
Suppose there is a single tree in this land: is it perceived by the preceding seven consciousnesses within a single moment of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), or is it not?
Is it conceptualized, or is it not conceptualized? This is precisely that single limit (*ekānta*).

In the interim, one attains the mutual functioning of the six sense organs; naturally wondrous and marvelous, one does not fall into the trap of seeking merit or achievement, which is called "Ultimate Bliss.
Furthermore, Śāriputra... [up to] "accomplishing such adornments of meritorious virtue."
The seven-jeweled ponds filled with water of eight virtues represent the dharma-style of Sukhāvatī.
Because the eight consciousnesses are subsumed into a single essence yet divided into manifold phenomena, they are called "jewels.
As for the water of eight virtues, it flows forth from within the *ālayavijñāna*; being entirely composed of immeasurable treasures, it causes sentient beings neither to wither nor to stagnate.
The ground where immeasurable wondrous functions abide is likewise composed entirely of golden sand; these fine sands represent wondrous functions.
The stairways and paths on all four sides symbolize earth, water, fire, and wind. Above them stands a multi-storied pavilion, which represents solely the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
All of this is the immeasurable wisdom of various kinds within the Tathāgatagarbha—namely, gold, silver, and even agate—which symbolizes the wondrousness within the primordial limit (*koṭi*).
Using the lotuses in the pond as an analogy, it is said that the Dharma is subtle and wondrous, as large as a chariot wheel; it is said that the Dharma is non-abiding.

From blue with blue light to white with white light, because the Dharma has its fundamental positions without confusion, it is subtly fragrant and pure, causing sentient beings to love and delight in it.
Were it otherwise, it would be like the aforementioned external conditions of kings, nobles, wealth, and status.
Even those who dwell in such households may practice this; how could it be that only a pure land is so?
Furthermore, Śāriputra... [up to] ...accomplishing such adornments of merit.
He once manifested celestial music to represent the phrases of the dhāraṇī; like the natural wondrousness of musical tones, so it is in this land.

The sound of music necessarily relies on the instrument to produce its tone; it is not human speech, yet it is not as if it were not human speech—it can be understood only by musicians, while others cannot know it.
The Buddha’s secret words are like the sound of music: those who awaken will understand them, while those who are deluded remain ignorant.
Why is this? Because they directly point to the phrase "Amitābha Buddha’s immeasurable light," which is identical to music.
Because sounds and phrases are non-dual and without duality, they cause sentient beings to be unconceivably perfumed and to naturally believe in and delight in that land.
Furthermore, the fact that there are heavens, earth, and the six periods of time therein means that the two lands—the pure and the defiled—are non-dual in their very essence.
Thus, at the time of a single meal, one makes offerings to ten trillion Buddha-lands, presenting flowers before each and every Buddha.
They prostrated and requested him to preach the essential Dharma, yet he did not emerge to receive their food for this duration; that one kalpa in this land is but a single day in that land.
This is neither due to supernatural powers nor the method of prolonging or shortening time—it is simply the natural state (*dharmatā*).
All of it is manifested solely by the mind: the experience of many kalpas is but a single day, a single day is but a moment, and a moment is but [a fraction of] a moment.
Since a single moment of abiding in this land lacks both coming and going, how could such a supremely excellent realm not be joyful?
Regarding the previous statement that the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* Buddhas preach the Dharma, the subsequent statement refers to the *dharmakāya* Buddha preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, [up to] "accomplishing such adornments of merit. Regarding the multicolored birds, the nets of trees, and so forth:

when these birds expound upon the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the five powers (*pañcabala*), they refer to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) that assist the path in this land; in that land, they are simply called the "five."
The mention of the "five faculties" (pañcendriya) and "five powers" (pañcabala) and so forth refers to the profundity of the power of that path. Why is this?

Because the inhabitants of that land rely on the non-self of both the environment and its inhabitants (dharmas and persons), they do not speak of suffering or pleasure; therefore, there are no four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni).

Furthermore, because the sentient beings of that country transcend both good and evil and are ever-pure, they do not speak of subduing evil or cultivating good; therefore, there are no four right efforts (catvāri samyakprahāṇāni).
Because of the Dharma, that land naturally possesses various adornments of merit and wisdom for those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
It is not said that they possess desire and so forth; thus, there are no four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Why is this? It is because they directly attain the supreme Dharma. However, that which clarifies this supreme Dharma is precisely within a single matter: concealing the body in every single thing.
They merely manifest the most supreme Dharma. In that Buddha-land, there are no three evil realms;

these various birds are all emanations produced by the Buddha, for the vow-power of Amitābha Buddha is vast and profound. If one discusses the ultimate principle, every dharma and every instance is none other than the manifestation of this single phrase:
"Amitābha Buddha. Thus, even the warbling of the oriole and the chirping of the magpie are included within this assembly.
The clamor of flowing water and the movement of the wind are all entirely mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha;

there is nothing that is not the manifestation of the eternal quiescent light (*śānta-prabhāsvara*). If one does not yet realize this, one must certainly make a vow to be born in that land in future lives.
Thus, all sufferings are extinguished and all joys manifest. This inconceivable Pure Land exists within a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*); it is not something external.
To attain neither attainment nor non-attainment, and not to destroy this characteristic—that is to establish the markless true characteristic (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*).
This precisely reveals that insentient things preach the Dharma. When the jeweled trees and jeweled nets are produced simultaneously, there is no sequential arising;
thus, the two lands of east and west, throughout the entirety of the empty *dharmadhātu*, are all established upon the tip of a single hair, wherein various seeds of the Dharma are arrayed.
All these various matters are entirely mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha. Why is this?
Because all various dharmas and their characteristics abide within the primordial limit (*koṭi*); being without before or after, they are said to act simultaneously and together.
Śāriputra, what do you think? [From here until: "Therefore he is named Amitābha.
Amitābha Buddha, having cultivated the radiance of immeasurable life for immeasurable kalpas, has realized the fruit of sainthood without obstruction.

While the preceding [passage] described the adornment of the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vyūha* and *sambhoga-vyūha*), this alone reveals his primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*). That is, Amitā...

The Buddha, within a single mote of dust, illumines the lands of the ten directions, penetrating all without obstruction; yet the four noble beings and the six classes of ordinary beings do not depart from that single mote of dust.
Why is this? Because the mote of dust is the most subtle of things, and for those of the highest capacity, it does not destroy the characteristic of the single mote of dust;
thus it is called vast and great. Being neither identical with nor separate from it, it is named "subtle and wondrous. Thus it is said.
The highest and most vast body of Amitābha Buddha also dwells within this minute speck of dust, preaching the Dharma and delivering sentient beings;

it can expand and it can contract, and is therefore called the "Infinite Meaning. Without passing even a moment, the Buddha’s lifespan is infinite and the lifespan of sentient beings is likewise infinite, all without departing from a single speck of dust.
If one can truly penetrate the meaning of the minute speck of dust, one will master the entirety of the *Dhāraṇī*.
The meaning of these phrases is self-evident.

Śāriputra, [up to] "accomplishing such adornments of merit," it means that in that Buddha-land there are only bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, and for ten kalpas there has been no populace with evil habits.
Because he has been born, he is said to be "accomplished" in such adornments of merit.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, [this] can only be described through immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers.
To speak of those who are "wondrously born" in that land, they immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression as those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

As for the people of this land, if they simply bring to mind the name of a single Buddha—without conceptual thought or effort—and continue this recitation until the end of their lives, they will naturally be born in that land of non-retrogression.
Whether it be a single recitation, ten recitations, or from one day up to seven days, by means of a single phrase of the Buddha’s name...
One who forms such a thought as "to sever the mind, intellect, and consciousness" will immediately give rise to the highest grade of superior power and shall not regress through their own strength.
As previously stated, that one birth of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) leading to birth without regression does not mean that sentient beings themselves do not regress;

rather, they are all sustained by the vow-power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. These are lands inhabited by sages and worthies where there are no evil companions; for this reason, [one does not regress].
It is not that one does not retreat; it is because this land is where ordinary beings and sages dwell together, and there are sentient beings who are evil.
Thus, encountering the good, one becomes good, and meeting the evil, one becomes evil; for this reason, there is the difficulty of advancing and retreating.
Śāriputra (up to: you should make a vow to be born in that land.
This person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha must necessarily vow to be reborn there. From one day up to seven days, they should simply refrain from even a single phrase;
when the Buddha appears before them, they do not see either the one who contemplates or the object of contemplation, nor is there even a thinker—this refers to refraining from even a single phrase.
If one does not know that the entire body is itself Buddha, yet contemplates in this manner, only then can one correspond with the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation.

One may thus enjoy the ground of leisure and bliss throughout one’s life; at the moment of death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of sages, will personally descend to welcome and guide one.
Because there is such great benefit, these words were spoken for the sake of the sentient beings in this land.
Those who hear this teaching should make a vow. If one lacks faith and aspiration, the many sufferings of this land will be difficult to endure and bear;
one will dwell long in the three miserable realms, with afflictions as companions and ignorance as a partner—when will such a person be liberated?
The Buddha said: "One cannot be born in that land by means of few roots of goodness or causes and conditions of merit; it requires the power of faith."
The power of mindfulness is such that when a person’s merit is fully perfected, all obstacles are naturally eliminated; it happens without being sought, and one simply sits upon a lotus flower.
This concludes the *Śāriputra-sūtra on Being Protected and Mindfully Remembered by All Buddhas*.
The same applies to the southern direction up to the zenith; as the names of the Buddhas and their lands therein are not yet detailed, they are not explained here.
(This note was originally written after the commentary on the text, but was erroneously transcribed here.)
"Śāriputra, what do you think? (Up to: You should all believe and accept my words and those spoken by all the Buddhas.
This is the truthful speech spoken within the Great Skillful Means of the World-Honored One;

yet, fearing that the sentient beings of this land might not believe in the benefits of inconceivable merit, the Buddha acts as a witness—namely, his broad and long tongue which completely covers [the world]."

Within this trichiliocosm, by those with the broad and long tongue—whether sentient or insentient, flowing water, or moving wind—all are gathered within the inconceivable dharma of non-duality, and therein they all recollect the Buddha, recollect the Dharma, and recollect the Sangha. Why is this?
It is because within a single atom, within the establishment of the dharma of non-duality, one speaks of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
Since all his words accord with the True Dharma, it is said that he speaks words of truth. In sum, these flow from a single word without preceding or succeeding syllables;
this reveals that the Dharmakāya Buddha teaches the most supreme Dharma, and thus it is called "inconceivable.
That which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas refers to the protection and mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions. "All Buddhas" means the various Buddhas.
They are all one and the same pure land. This pure land is simply that which all Buddhas and sentient beings inherently possess;
it is not obtained from without. After three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of removing defilement and returning to purity, one arrives at the pure land of one's own mind.
Therefore, no further effort is required, for it is naturally protected and sustained by mindfulness.
Śāriputra (and the others) paid homage and withdrew.

Thus it is that by recollecting the Buddha, one’s transgressions are extinguished and merit arises; once the sprout of the seed of Bodhi has been planted, if one does not make a vow, one will not reach the Pure Land.
By sitting upon a lotus flower for the duration of a single finger-snap, one shall behold Amitābha Buddha and immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.
As for the statement that "the Ear of the Earth has already made its vow," and that "now [I] make a vow known to all people"—as for why those who ought to make a vow are remembered so early:

it is because such things occur among the foolish. There are those who make a vow but do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha, and there are those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha but do not make a vow;
therefore, one must make a vow precisely for this reason. If the power of mindfulness and the power of the vow...
